question: Which peace settlement ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648?
explanation: The Peace of Westphalia, negotiated in Münster and Osnabrück, ended the war in 1648.

question: Which king made Versailles the seat of his court and was known as the Sun King?
explanation: Louis XIV moved the court to Versailles in 1682 and, as the Sun King, became the embodiment of absolutism.

question: What did Isaac Newton describe in his Principia of 1687?
choices: The laws of motion and gravitation
explanation: With his laws of motion and his law of gravitation, Newton explained the movement of bodies on Earth and in space.

question: Which city did Peter the Great found in 1703 as the new capital of Russia?
explanation: St. Petersburg on the Neva became the capital in 1712 and was regarded as Russia's window on Europe.

question: Which two powers were on the same side in the Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763)?
explanation: Prussia under Frederick II and Great Britain fought together against Austria, France and Russia.

question: With which motto did Immanuel Kant sum up the program of the Enlightenment?
choices: Have the courage to use your own understanding
explanation: In 1784 Kant defined enlightenment as the emergence from self-imposed immaturity and chose Sapere aude as its motto.

question: Why was Galileo Galilei condemned by the Inquisition in 1633?
choices: Because he had invented the telescope
Because he had translated the Bible into Italian
Because he had defended the heliocentric view of the universe
explanation: In his Dialogue of 1632 Galileo had supported the teaching of Copernicus that the Earth moves around the Sun; he was forced to recant.

question: What happened to the English king Charles I in 1649?
choices: He was condemned by Parliament and executed
explanation: After the civil war a court of Parliament convicted the king of high treason; he was beheaded on January 30, 1649.

question: Which demand is associated with Montesquieu's work The Spirit of the Laws (1748)?
explanation: Montesquieu called for the legislative, executive and judicial powers to be separated so that they would limit one another.

question: What was the consequence of the Edict of Fontainebleau of 1685?
choices: The founding of the Royal Society
The move of the court to Versailles
The beginning of the War of the Spanish Succession
The flight of some 200,000 Huguenots from France
explanation: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and banned Protestant worship; many Huguenots fled, among other places to Brandenburg.

question: Which country sealed itself off almost completely from the outside world from 1639 onward and allowed only the Dutch to trade on the island of Dejima?
explanation: The Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity and restricted foreign trade to Nagasaki; this policy is called sakoku.

question: Which achievement is associated with the physicist Émilie du Châtelet?
choices: The discovery of the moons of Jupiter
The French translation and explanation of Newton's Principia
explanation: Du Châtelet translated Newton's main work into French and added commentaries; her version is still regarded as authoritative today.

question: In which city did the first democracy emerge in the 6th and 5th centuries BC?
explanation: In Athens the reforms of Cleisthenes laid the foundation of popular rule in 508 BC.

question: Where were the first recorded Olympic Games held in 776 BC?
explanation: The games were held every four years at Olympia in the Peloponnese in honor of Zeus.

question: Which battle decided the second Persian War at sea in 480 BC?
explanation: Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow bay of Salamis, where the Greek triremes prevailed.

question: Who won the Peloponnesian War, which ended in 404 BC?
explanation: With Persian money Sparta built a fleet and forced Athens to surrender in 404 BC.

question: Which philosopher was the teacher of Alexander the Great?
explanation: Aristotle taught the young Alexander at the Macedonian court before founding the Lyceum in Athens.

question: Which event is regarded as the end of the Hellenistic age?
choices: The destruction of Corinth in 146 BC
The death of Cleopatra and the annexation of Egypt in 30 BC
The death of Alexander in 323 BC
The Battle of Pydna in 168 BC
explanation: With the suicide of Cleopatra VII, Egypt, the last Hellenistic kingdom, passed to Rome.

question: Which reform did Solon carry out in Athens around 594 BC?
choices: He gave women the right to vote
explanation: Solon cancelled debts and forbade the enslavement of citizens for debt; he divided the citizens into four classes according to wealth.

question: Who led the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae in 480 BC?
explanation: King Leonidas held the pass against the army of Xerxes with his Spartans and allies until every one of them had fallen.

question: Which poet from the island of Lesbos did Plato call the tenth Muse?
explanation: Around 600 BC Sappho wrote songs about love and longing; only fragments of her nine books survive.

question: Which temple was built on the Acropolis under Pericles between 447 and 432 BC?
explanation: The Parthenon, built by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates, was dedicated to the goddess Athena and housed a twelve-meter statue by Phidias.

question: What were Alexander's generals called, who fought over his empire after his death?
explanation: The Diadochi, the successors, waged war from 322 to 281 BC; in the end came the empires of the Ptolemies, the Seleucids and the Antigonids.

question: Which scholar was killed in 212 BC during the Roman capture of Syracuse?
explanation: Archimedes had supported the defense of his home city with war machines; a Roman soldier killed him against the orders of Marcellus.

question: Who founded the Persian Empire of the Achaemenids around 550 BC?
explanation: Cyrus II defeated the Medes and went on to conquer Lydia and Babylon; Darius and Xerxes were later Great Kings.

question: Which teaching did Siddhartha Gautama proclaim in northern India?
explanation: As the Buddha, the Awakened One, Siddhartha Gautama became the founder of Buddhism.

question: What, among other things, did Qin Shi Huang standardize after the unification of China in 221 BC?
explanation: The First Emperor introduced uniform characters, coins, measures, weights and axle widths in order to hold the empire together.

question: Which invention is attributed to the Chinese court official Cai Lun in the year 105?
explanation: In 105 Cai Lun described an improved process for making paper from bark, hemp and rags.

question: Which mathematical innovation arose in India in the time of the Gupta Empire?
explanation: Indian mathematicians of the Gupta period developed the decimal system with the digit zero, which reached Europe by way of the Arab world.

question: Under which king was Angkor Wat built in the 12th century?
explanation: The Khmer king Suryavarman II had Angkor Wat built as a temple to Vishnu and as his own tomb.

question: To which sage is the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Daoism, attributed?
explanation: The Tao Te Ching is regarded as the work of the legendary Laozi; Zhuangzi was a later Daoist thinker, while Confucius and Mengzi represented Confucianism.

question: What is the name of the work by the strategist Sun Tzu from the period of the Warring States?
explanation: Sun Tzu's Art of War, in thirteen chapters, teaches that the best victory is won without a battle.

question: What was remarkable about the reign of Wu Zetian from 690 to 705?
choices: She was the only woman in China to rule as empress in her own right
She had the Terracotta Army made
explanation: In 690 Wu Zetian proclaimed a dynasty of her own and is the only woman in Chinese history to have borne the imperial title herself.

question: Why is the Diamond Sutra of 868 so important for the history of printing?
choices: It was printed with movable metal type
It is the first book made of paper
It is the oldest surviving printed text bearing a precise date
It was used by Gutenberg as a model
explanation: The colophon of the scroll, printed from woodblocks, gives the date May 11, 868; it is thus the oldest dated printed book in the world.

question: Which empire did Ardashir I replace in Persia in the year 224?
explanation: In 224 Ardashir I defeated the last Parthian king and founded the Sasanian Empire, which lasted until 651.

question: Who wrote the Shiji around 100 BC, the first comprehensive work of Chinese historiography?
explanation: The court historian Sima Qian wrote the Shiji in 130 chapters; Cai Lun improved paper, Zhang Qian was an envoy and Xuanzang a Buddhist pilgrim.

question: Which event triggered the First World War in the summer of 1914?
explanation: The murder of the Austrian heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, on June 28, 1914 in Sarajevo led through the July Crisis into war.

question: Who led the Bolsheviks to power in the October Revolution of 1917?
explanation: Lenin returned from exile in April 1917 and in November led the overthrow in Petrograd.

question: On which day did the Armistice of Compiègne come into force?
explanation: The armistice came into force at 11 o'clock on November 11, 1918 and ended the fighting on the Western Front.

question: Which great power never joined the League of Nations, although its president had proposed it?
explanation: The American Senate rejected membership, although Woodrow Wilson had outlined the League of Nations in his Fourteen Points.

question: Which reform was NOT part of Atatürk's transformation of Turkey?
explanation: Atatürk abolished the caliphate in 1924; he carried through the other reforms in the 1920s and 1930s.

question: What was Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 directed against?
choices: Against the import of British cloth
Against the British salt monopoly and the salt tax
explanation: Gandhi marched 385 kilometers to the sea and there demonstratively extracted salt, which was forbidden under British law.

question: Through which achievement did Mustafa Kemal become known in 1915?
choices: The defense of Gallipoli against the Allies
explanation: As a colonel, Mustafa Kemal and his troops held the heights of the Gallipoli peninsula; the Allies had to withdraw in January 1916.

question: Which new currency ended the hyperinflation in Germany in November 1923?
explanation: The Rentenmark, introduced on November 15, 1923, stabilized the currency; the Reichsmark replaced it in 1924.

question: Who was the first woman to give a speech in a German parliament, on February 19, 1919?
explanation: The Social Democrat Marie Juchacz spoke in the Weimar National Assembly and in the same year founded the Arbeiterwohlfahrt welfare organization.

question: Which school of art, craft and design did Walter Gropius found in Weimar in 1919?
explanation: The Bauhaus moved to Dessau in 1925 and was closed by the National Socialists in 1933; its influence on architecture and design continues to this day.

question: What did the stab-in-the-back myth claim after the First World War?
choices: That the Allies had broken the armistice
That the emperor had betrayed the army
That the army, undefeated in the field, had been betrayed by the home front and the politicians
That the reparations had been invented by France
explanation: Hindenburg and Ludendorff spread the myth in order to conceal their own responsibility for the defeat; it served the opponents of the republic as a propaganda weapon.

question: What is the name of the oldest known writing system in the world, developed by the Sumerians?
explanation: Around 3200 BC the Sumerians pressed wedge-shaped signs into clay tablets; hence the name cuneiform, from the Latin for wedge.

question: Which river was the lifeline of ancient Egypt?
explanation: The annual Nile flood brought fertile silt and made Egypt a rich agricultural land.

question: What is the Babylonian king Hammurabi best known for?
choices: For the invention of the wheel
explanation: Around 1750 BC Hammurabi had some 280 legal provisions recorded on a stele, the Code of Hammurabi.

question: Which pharaoh worshipped the sun disk Aten alone and founded the city of Akhetaten?
explanation: Akhenaten banned the old cults of the gods and moved the capital to Akhetaten, near present-day Amarna.

question: Between which powers was the oldest surviving peace treaty concluded after the Battle of Kadesh?
explanation: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III agreed on peace and mutual assistance about 15 years after the battle.

question: Which sources provide the oldest evidence of Chinese writing?
choices: Stone tablets of the Great Wall
Bamboo books of the Zhou period
Oracle bones of the Shang dynasty
explanation: The Shang kings scratched their questions to the ancestors into ox bones and turtle shells; these inscriptions are the oldest Chinese written records.

question: Who is regarded as the first author in world history known by name?
explanation: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess in Ur, names herself as the author in her hymns.

question: Which people developed an alphabet of 22 letters around 1050 BC that the Greeks later adopted?
explanation: The Phoenicians of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos simplified writing to 22 consonant signs; the Greeks added vowels.

question: What, among other things, is the Epic of Gilgamesh about?
explanation: After the death of his friend Enkidu, Gilgamesh seeks out Utnapishtim, the hero of the flood, in order to gain eternal life, and fails.

question: Which civilization built palaces such as Knossos on Crete?
explanation: The Minoans, named after the legendary king Minos, created the first advanced civilization in Europe from around 2000 BC.

question: What was remarkable about Fu Hao, the consort of the Shang king Wu Ding?
choices: As a woman she led armies into battle
She ruled as the first empress of China
She built the first Great Wall
explanation: Oracle bones report that Fu Hao commanded campaigns with thousands of soldiers; her unplundered tomb was discovered at Anyang in 1976.

question: Where was the kingdom of Kush, whose king Piye conquered Egypt around 730 BC?
choices: In Ethiopia on the Red Sea
explanation: Kush, with its capitals at Napata and later Meroe, lay south of Egypt on the Nile; its kings formed the 25th Dynasty.

question: Which invention is regarded as the most important driving force of the Industrial Revolution?
explanation: The steam engine, improved by James Watt, powered factories, locomotives and ships.

question: Who wrote the Communist Manifesto in 1848 together with Friedrich Engels?
explanation: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the Manifesto in London in February 1848.

question: In which year was the German Empire founded?
explanation: On January 18, 1871 Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

question: What was the result of the Meiji Restoration of 1868?
choices: India became a British crown colony
explanation: After the fall of the shogunate, Japan became an industrial power under Emperor Meiji within a single generation.

question: Which continent was divided among the European powers at the Berlin Conference of 1884/85?
explanation: The conference laid down rules for taking possession of African territory and set off the Scramble for Africa.

question: Which country had to cede Hong Kong to Great Britain after the First Opium War in 1842?
explanation: In the Treaty of Nanking China ceded Hong Kong and opened five ports to British trade.

question: Which country was the first in the world to introduce women's suffrage at the national level, in 1893?
explanation: After a petition with almost 32,000 signatures, the governor of New Zealand signed the electoral act on September 19, 1893.

question: Which book did Charles Darwin publish in 1859?
explanation: Darwin's main work explained the diversity of life through evolution and natural selection and sold out on the first day.

question: Who owned the Congo Free State from 1885 to 1908?
choices: King Leopold II of Belgium as personal property
explanation: Leopold II had the Congo exploited as his personal property; only after an international scandal did Belgium take over the colony in 1908.

question: Which insurance did the German Empire introduce in 1883 as its first social insurance?
explanation: Health insurance came in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and old-age and disability insurance in 1889; unemployment insurance did not follow until 1927.

question: Which experience led Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross?
choices: The wounded of the Battle of Solferino in 1859
explanation: In 1859 Dunant witnessed the misery of the wounded after the Battle of Solferino and in his book called for voluntary aid societies and a protective convention.

question: What was the consequence of the Sepoy Rebellion of 1857 for India?
choices: The British Crown took over rule from the East India Company
The Mughal emperor again ruled all of India
explanation: After the rebellion was put down, the East India Company was dissolved in 1858 and India was placed directly under the British Crown.

question: Which event marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar?
explanation: Muhammad's emigration from Mecca to Medina in the year 622 was fixed by Caliph Umar as the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

question: Who defeated an Arab-Berber army at Tours and Poitiers in 732?
explanation: In 732 the Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel halted the advance of Muslim troops to the north.

question: Which dynasty founded the city of Baghdad in 762?
explanation: In 762 the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur had the round city of Baghdad built on the Tigris as his new capital.

question: Which work made Ibn Sina (Avicenna) famous in Europe into the 17th century?
explanation: In Latin translation, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was for centuries the most important medical textbook at European universities.

question: In which year did Saladin recapture Jerusalem from the Crusaders?
explanation: After his victory at Hattin, Saladin took Jerusalem on October 2, 1187; the conquest by the First Crusade had taken place in 1099.

question: Who destroyed Baghdad in 1258 and ended the caliphate of the Abbasids?
explanation: The Mongol army of Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, captured Baghdad in 1258 and had the last Abbasid caliph executed.

question: Which event of 680 remains of central importance for Shiites to this day?
choices: The death of Husayn at Karbala
explanation: Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet, was killed at Karbala in 680 by troops of the Umayyad caliph Yazid; Shiites commemorate his death each year on the Day of Ashura.

question: Where does the word algebra come from?
choices: From the name of the city of Baghdad
From the name of the mathematician al-Khwarizmi
From the title of a book of calculation by al-Khwarizmi
explanation: Al-Khwarizmi's book on calculating by completion and balancing, in Arabic al-jabr, gave algebra its name; his own name, by contrast, gave rise to the word algorithm.

question: Which dynasty founded the city of Cairo in 969?
explanation: The Shiite Fatimids conquered Egypt in 969 and laid out the palace city of al-Qahira, which became Cairo; construction of the al-Azhar mosque began in 970.

question: What was the consequence of the Battle of Manzikert in 1071?
explanation: After the Seljuk victory over Byzantium, Turkic tribes settled Asia Minor, where the Sultanate of Rum and later the Ottoman Empire arose.

question: Who endowed the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez in 859, from which one of the oldest universities in the world developed?
explanation: Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a merchant, financed the building of the mosque out of her inheritance; the University of al-Qarawiyyin still exists today.

question: What happened in Granada on January 2, 1492?
choices: The last emir handed the city over to the Catholic Monarchs
explanation: With the surrender of Granada by Muhammad XII, known as Boabdil, to Isabella and Ferdinand, Muslim rule in Spain ended after almost 800 years.

question: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
explanation: On November 9, 1989 the GDR opened the border crossings; reunification followed on October 3, 1990.

question: Which crisis brought the world to the brink of nuclear war in 1962?
explanation: Soviet missiles in Cuba led in October 1962 to a thirteen-day confrontation between Kennedy and Khrushchev.

question: Who became president in South Africa's first free elections in 1994?
explanation: Nelson Mandela, who had spent 27 years in prison, became the first black president of South Africa after the election victory of the ANC.

question: By what method did Mahatma Gandhi win independence for India?
choices: Negotiations with the League of Nations
explanation: Gandhi relied on boycotts, marches such as the Salt March and nonviolent disobedience against British rule.

question: Which reform concepts are associated with Mikhail Gorbachev?
choices: Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution
explanation: With glasnost, openness, and perestroika, restructuring, Gorbachev attempted from 1985 onward to reform the Soviet Union.

question: Which event triggered the global financial crisis in 2008?
choices: China's accession to the World Trade Organization
The collapse of the bank Lehman Brothers
explanation: The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers on September 15, 2008 shook the worldwide financial system.

question: How did the Western powers respond to the Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948?
choices: They withdrew their troops from Berlin
They supplied the city by means of an airlift
They broke through the blockade with tanks
They imposed a naval blockade on the Soviet Union
explanation: For almost a year American and British aircraft flew coal, food and medicine into West Berlin, until Stalin lifted the blockade in May 1949.

question: Why is 1960 called the Year of Africa?
choices: Because apartheid in South Africa came to an end
Because the African Union was founded
Because the Suez Canal was nationalized
explanation: Within a single year 17 states gained independence, among them almost all the French colonies as well as Nigeria, Somalia and the Congo.

question: Which movement emerged from the Bandung Conference of 1955?
choices: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
explanation: At Bandung 29 Asian and African states called for a path of their own between the blocs; in 1961 they founded the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade.

question: What did Rosa Parks do in 1955 to set off the Montgomery bus boycott?
choices: She gave a speech before Congress
She went on hunger strike in prison
She refused to give up her seat to a white passenger
She filed a lawsuit against the city of Montgomery
explanation: Parks remained seated on the bus and was arrested; the black population then boycotted the city's buses for 381 days.

question: What does the policy of Deng Xiaoping from 1978 onward stand for?
choices: For the break with the Soviet Union
For reform and opening toward a market economy
explanation: Deng permitted private enterprise, created special economic zones and opened China to foreign capital, but held fast to the sole rule of the party.

question: In which year did the Vietnam War end with the capture of Saigon by the North?
explanation: The USA withdrew in 1973; on April 30, 1975 North Vietnamese troops took Saigon and united the country under communist rule.

question: Who was crowned emperor in Rome at Christmas in the year 800?
explanation: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in St. Peter's on December 25, 800.

question: Which event is regarded as the beginning of the Viking Age?
choices: The raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793
explanation: The raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in the year 793 caused horror across Europe and marks the beginning of the Viking Age.

question: What did the Magna Carta of 1215 lay down?
choices: The division of the Frankish Empire
The election of the pope by cardinals
That the king is bound by the law and may levy no taxes without consent
The founding of the University of Oxford
explanation: King John had to assure the barons that no one would be imprisoned without judgment and that no tax would be levied without the consent of the council.

question: Which empire did Mansa Musa rule, who made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324?
explanation: Mansa Musa was king of the West African Mali Empire, which controlled the gold trade across the Sahara.

question: Which city did Joan of Arc liberate in 1429 during the Hundred Years' War?
explanation: In May 1429 Joan of Arc ended the English siege of Orléans and afterward led the Dauphin to Reims for his coronation.

question: Which sultan conquered Constantinople in 1453?
explanation: Mehmed II, called the Conqueror, took Constantinople on May 29, 1453 and made it the capital of the Ottoman Empire.

question: Which king waited as a penitent before the castle of Canossa in 1077 for the pope's forgiveness?
explanation: During the Investiture Controversy, Henry IV asked Pope Gregory VII at Canossa to release him from the excommunication the pope had imposed on him in 1076.

question: What did the Treaty of Verdun lay down in 843?
choices: The imperial coronation of Otto I
The end of the Viking raids
The division of the Frankish Empire among the grandsons of Charlemagne
The founding of the Hanseatic League
explanation: At Verdun, Charles the Bald, Louis the German and Lothair I divided the Frankish Empire into a western, an eastern and a middle kingdom.

question: Which emperor had the Hagia Sophia built in Constantinople between 532 and 537?
explanation: Justinian I had the Hagia Sophia rebuilt after the Nika revolt and consecrated it in 537; for almost a thousand years it was the largest church in the world.

question: Whom did Otto I defeat on the Lechfeld near Augsburg in the year 955?
explanation: In 955 Otto I defeated the Hungarian mounted warriors who had been plundering central Europe for decades, and he was crowned emperor in 962.

question: Which ruler turned the city-state of Cusco into the Inca Empire from about 1438 onward?
explanation: Pachacuti defeated the Chanka, expanded Cusco into a capital and founded the empire of Tawantinsuyu; Atahualpa was the last Inca before the Spanish conquest.

question: What did the stone city of Great Zimbabwe in southern Africa live on above all between the 13th and 15th centuries?
choices: On the salt trade across the Sahara
On the silk trade with Byzantium
On the gold and ivory trade with the Swahili Coast
On the fur trade with Novgorod
explanation: The rulers of Great Zimbabwe controlled gold deposits and herds of cattle and traded through ports such as Kilwa and Sofala as far as India and China.

question: Which invention is attributed to Johannes Gutenberg around 1450?
explanation: In Mainz, Gutenberg developed printing with individually cast letters and a printing press.

question: In which year did Christopher Columbus reach America?
explanation: Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas on October 12, 1492.

question: What were Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 directed against first and foremost?
choices: Against the translation of the Bible
explanation: Luther criticized the practice of buying one's way out of punishment for sin through the purchase of letters of indulgence.

question: Which empire did the Spanish conquer in 1521 with the fall of Tenochtitlan?
explanation: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztecs; Hernán Cortés conquered it after a siege lasting months.

question: Which innovation did Nicolaus Copernicus advance in his work of 1543?
choices: The Earth revolves around the Sun
explanation: Copernicus placed the Sun at the center; the elliptical orbits were not discovered until Kepler.

question: What was the purpose of the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563)?
choices: The election of a new pope
The clarification of Catholic doctrine in response to the Reformation
explanation: The council reaffirmed Catholic doctrine against the Protestants and resolved on internal reforms of the church.

question: What did the Treaty of Tordesillas lay down in 1494?
choices: The border between France and the Empire
The division of the world between Spain and Portugal
explanation: Along a line in the Atlantic, new lands to the west were to belong to Spain and those to the east to Portugal; this is why Brazil fell to Portugal.

question: Which principle did the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 lay down?
choices: The territorial ruler determines the confession of his territory
Every subject freely chooses his religion
Only Catholicism is permitted in the Empire
The emperor decides the faith of all princes
explanation: Each imperial estate was allowed to choose between the Catholic and the Lutheran confession for its territory; those of another faith were permitted to emigrate.

question: Which city was a center of learning in the Songhai Empire under Askia Mohammed?
explanation: Timbuktu on the Niger, with its Sankoré mosque, was a center of Islamic scholarship and of trade across the Sahara.

question: Who founded the Jesuit order in 1540?
explanation: The former soldier Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which was confirmed by the pope in 1540.

question: What happened at the Diet of Worms in 1521?
choices: Luther refused to recant his teachings
The Peace of Augsburg was concluded
explanation: Before Emperor Charles V, Luther declared that he could recant only if he were refuted from the Bible; he was thereupon outlawed.

question: Which ruler governed the Mughal Empire in India from 1556 and was known for his religious tolerance?
explanation: Akbar abolished the special tax on non-Muslims and had representatives of all religions debate at his court.

question: Which event is regarded as the beginning of the French Revolution?
choices: The Battle of the Nations at Leipzig
explanation: The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789 is regarded as the opening of the Revolution; July 14 is France's national holiday today.

question: Which colonies declared their independence from Great Britain in 1776?
choices: The Spanish colonies in South America
Thirteen British colonies in North America
explanation: The thirteen colonies on the North American east coast founded the United States of America.

question: Who led the insurgents in the Haitian Revolution?
explanation: The former slave Toussaint Louverture became the most important leader of the uprising in Saint-Domingue.

question: What was the Code civil of 1804?
choices: A uniform civil code for France
explanation: The Code civil unified civil law and established equality before the law, property and freedom of contract.

question: Which statesman shaped the Congress of Vienna of 1814 to 1815 most decisively?
explanation: The Austrian foreign minister Metternich presided over the congress and stood for the policy of Restoration.

question: Why did the Frankfurt National Assembly fail in 1849?
choices: It could not agree on any basic rights
The Prussian king refused the imperial crown
explanation: In 1849 Frederick William IV refused the imperial crown offered by the parliament; the National Assembly then fell apart.

question: In which city was the Constitution of the United States adopted in 1787?
explanation: From May to September 1787, 55 delegates deliberated on the constitution in Philadelphia under the chairmanship of George Washington; the capital Washington was not built until later.

question: What did the women of Paris achieve with their march to Versailles in October 1789?
choices: The right to vote for women
explanation: The women forced Louis XVI to sign the Declaration of the Rights of Man and to move with his family from Versailles to Paris, where he stood before the eyes of the people.

question: Which find from Napoleon's Egyptian campaign made the decipherment of the hieroglyphs possible?
explanation: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, bears the same text in hieroglyphs, demotic script and Greek; with it Champollion achieved the decipherment in 1822.

question: What happened on August 6, 1806?
choices: Prussia lost the Battle of Jena
The Confederation of the Rhine was founded
Francis II laid down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire
explanation: After the founding of the Confederation of the Rhine and an ultimatum from Napoleon, Francis II declared the more than 800-year-old empire dissolved.

question: Whose arrival decided the Battle of Waterloo on the evening of June 18, 1815?
choices: The Russian Guard under Tsar Alexander
explanation: Wellington's army held out all day until Blücher's Prussians arrived and put Napoleon's army to flight.

question: Which work did Mary Wollstonecraft publish in 1792?
choices: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
The Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen
explanation: In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Wollstonecraft demanded equal education and civil rights for women; the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen is the work of Olympe de Gouges.

question: In which year was Rome founded according to legend?
explanation: Roman tradition gives 753 BC as the year of the founding by Romulus.

question: Against which city did Rome wage the three Punic Wars?
explanation: Carthage in North Africa was Rome's great rival and was destroyed in 146 BC.

question: What happened on the Ides of March in 44 BC?
choices: Rome was captured by the Gauls
explanation: Senators around Brutus and Cassius stabbed Caesar to death on March 15, 44 BC.

question: What is the form of rule established by Augustus called?
explanation: Augustus ruled as princeps, the first among equals; hence the Principate.

question: Which emperor granted the Christians freedom of religion in 313?
explanation: In 313 Constantine and Licinius agreed in Milan on the free exercise of religion.

question: Who deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476?
explanation: The Germanic commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and became king of Italy.

question: What was the Law of the Twelve Tables of around 450 BC?
explanation: Under pressure from the plebeians the law was recorded on twelve tables and put on public display in the Forum.

question: Who led the greatest slave revolt of antiquity from 73 to 71 BC?
explanation: The gladiator Spartacus escaped from Capua and led tens of thousands of slaves until Crassus defeated him in 71 BC.

question: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its greatest extent in 117?
explanation: Trajan conquered Dacia, Armenia and Mesopotamia; his successor Hadrian gave up the eastern conquests again.

question: What did the Constitutio Antoniniana of the emperor Caracalla lay down in the year 212?
choices: The division of the empire into four parts
The transfer of the capital to Constantinople
Roman citizenship for almost all free inhabitants of the empire
explanation: The edict made millions of provincial inhabitants Roman citizens; Roman law now applied throughout the empire.

question: Which form of rule did Diocletian introduce in 293?
explanation: In the Tetrarchy two emperors and two junior emperors ruled the empire together, in order to defend the frontiers more effectively.

question: Which scholar was murdered by a Christian mob in Alexandria in 415?
explanation: The mathematician and philosopher Hypatia became caught up in the power struggle between the city prefect and Bishop Cyril and was killed.

question: On which continent did modern humans, Homo sapiens, emerge?
explanation: The oldest fossils of Homo sapiens come from Africa and are around 300,000 years old.

question: What is meant by the Neolithic Revolution?
choices: The transition to farming, animal husbandry and settled life
The migration of humans out of Africa
explanation: In the Neolithic, people began to cultivate plants and breed animals, and lived permanently in villages.

question: What is the cave of Lascaux in France known for?
choices: For Ice Age paintings of animals
For the skeleton of a Neanderthal
For the first finds of grain
explanation: At Lascaux, people painted hundreds of horses, aurochs and deer on the cave walls about 17,000 years ago.

question: How did the first humans reach America?
choices: Over a land bridge from Africa
Over the Bering land bridge from Siberia to Alaska
explanation: During the Ice Age the sea level was so low that there was solid land between Siberia and Alaska.

question: How did Ötzi, the Iceman, die?
choices: From a fall into a crevasse
From freezing to death in a snowstorm
explanation: An arrowhead in his left shoulder shows that Ötzi was killed.

question: What is remarkable about Göbekli Tepe in present-day Turkey?
choices: It is the oldest city with a city wall
Monumental stone circles were erected there while people were still hunters and gatherers
The oldest cuneiform tablets were found there
explanation: The T-shaped pillars of Göbekli Tepe were created around 9500 BC, before farming and animal husbandry had taken hold in the region.

question: Which human species was the first to leave Africa and spread as far as Java and China?
explanation: Homo erectus reached the Caucasus about 1.8 million years ago and later East and Southeast Asia.

question: Where were the oldest known clay vessels in the world made?
explanation: Sherds from the Xianrendong Cave in southern China are around 18,000 to 20,000 years old and still come from hunters and gatherers.

question: What is the Blombos Cave in South Africa known for?
choices: For the oldest engraved patterns and ornamental beads
For the first finds of grain
explanation: In the Blombos Cave, pieces of ochre around 75,000 years old bearing geometric patterns and pierced snail shells were found.

question: How were the Denisovans discovered?
choices: Through a complete skeleton in Siberia
Through cave paintings in the Altai
Through DNA analysis of a finger bone
explanation: In 2010 the genome of a previously unknown human species was obtained from a tiny finger bone from the Denisova Cave.

question: Which settlement in the Jordan Valley was given a stone wall and a tower around 8000 BC?
explanation: Jericho is regarded as one of the oldest permanently inhabited settlements in the world; the tower is almost nine meters high.

question: By what do archaeologists recognize the seafarers who settled the Pacific islands from about 1500 BC onward?
explanation: The Lapita culture is named after a site in New Caledonia; its characteristically decorated pottery marks the path of settlement as far as Tonga and Samoa.

question: With which event did the Second World War begin in Europe?
choices: The attack on the Soviet Union
explanation: On September 1, 1939 the Wehrmacht attacked Poland; two days later Great Britain and France declared war on Germany.

question: How many Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
explanation: The National Socialists murdered around six million European Jews, as well as hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities and other groups.

question: Which battle is regarded as the turning point of the war on the Eastern Front?
explanation: With the surrender of the Sixth Army at Stalingrad in February 1943, the Wehrmacht went permanently on the defensive in the East.

question: What was discussed at the Wannsee Conference in January 1942?
choices: The attack on the Soviet Union
The organization of the deportation and murder of the European Jews
explanation: Under the direction of Reinhard Heydrich, the SS and government ministries coordinated the so-called Final Solution of the Jewish Question.

question: To which resistance group did Sophie and Hans Scholl belong?
explanation: The White Rose distributed leaflets against the Nazi regime in Munich; the Scholl siblings were executed in 1943.

question: Which date is regarded as the end of the Second World War in Europe?
explanation: On May 8, 1945 the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht came into force; Japan did not capitulate until September 2.

question: What did Germany and the Soviet Union agree in the secret additional protocol of the Hitler-Stalin Pact of August 1939?
choices: A joint attack on Great Britain
The division of Poland and Eastern Europe into spheres of interest
The exchange of prisoners of war
explanation: The protocol divided Poland along the rivers Narew, Vistula and San and assigned Finland, the Baltic states and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere.

question: Who set off the bomb at the Wolf's Lair Führer headquarters on July 20, 1944?
explanation: Colonel Stauffenberg placed the briefcase with the explosive at the situation briefing; Hitler survived slightly injured, and Stauffenberg was shot that same night.

question: What happened after the capture of Nanking in December 1937?
choices: Japanese troops murdered tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of civilians and prisoners over a period of weeks
The city was declared the capital of Japan
The League of Nations sent peacekeeping troops
explanation: The Nanking Massacre lasted about six weeks; the Tokyo Tribunal assumed more than 200,000 dead, and mass rape was part of the crime.

question: Which charge was tried for the first time before an international court at the Nuremberg Trials of 1945/46?
explanation: Alongside war crimes and crimes against peace, the tribunal introduced the new offense of crimes against humanity, which shapes international criminal law to this day.

question: Which territory did Czechoslovakia cede to Germany after the Munich Agreement of 1938?
explanation: Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany agreed, without the participation of Czechoslovakia, on the cession of the largely German-speaking Sudetenland.

question: Which theologian of the Confessing Church was executed at the Flossenbürg concentration camp in April 1945?
explanation: Bonhoeffer had joined the resistance through the Abwehr and was hanged on April 9, 1945 on Hitler's orders; Niemöller survived the Dachau concentration camp.
